vertices.title: efSearch for the recall target
vertices.note:
The sweep is in bench/ann-sweep.md but nobody has written down
what it means. This is the decision the demo makes.

vertices.title: How many shards, and how are results merged?

edges.answer:
Approximate. A brute-force scan over 48M x 768 fp32 reads
140 GB a query and lands at 400 ms, eight times the latency budget.
edges.falsifier: a brute-force scan lands under the 50 ms budget at this corpus size -- a GPU implementation is the candidate

edges.answer:
*HNSW*, M=32, efConstruction=200.

The sweep, from [[file:bench/ann-sweep.md][the sweep]]:

| index  | recall@10 | p99 (ms) |  RAM |
|--------+-----------+----------+------|
| flat   |     1.000 |      410 | 140G |
| IVF-PQ |     0.918 |        6 |  12G |
| HNSW   |     0.962 |       11 |  61G |

IVF-PQ is four points of recall cheaper than we can afford, so =HNSW= it is.
This constrains [[dg:D04][D04]]: efSearch is what buys the last of that
recall back, and it is paid for in latency.
edges.falsifier: recall@10 against exact search falls below 0.95 on the held-out queries

edges.answer:
Cosine, on vectors the encoder has already L2-normalised.
Inner product ranks identically on normalised vectors, and every eval
script already assumes cosine.

The exact scan, kept as an offline oracle: top-100 for a frozen
5k query set, recomputed whenever the encoder changes.
